questions.q: What should be the very first thing you run in your capstone reproduction, before any of your own code?
options: The write-up report template
Your own reimplementation of the model from scratch
The authors' official, unmodified code with their own default command
A hyperparameter sweep across many learning rates
questions.explain: The reproduction playbook from Lesson 7 requires confirming the official code reproduces its own claimed number in your environment before any of your own code is introduced.

questions.q: The paper's prose and the authors' released code disagree about a hyperparameter value. Which should you use?
options: Always use the value stated in the paper's prose
Average the two values
Skip that hyperparameter entirely
Use the code's actual value and note the discrepancy
questions.explain: The code is the ground truth for what was actually run; the paper is a lossy summary. When they disagree, use the code's value and record the discrepancy rather than silently picking one.

questions.q: When should you initialize your experiment tracker (W&B or MLflow) relative to your training runs?
options: Only after a run looks promising, to avoid cluttering the project
Tracking is optional if you keep careful notes by hand
From the very first attempt, with the full config logged alongside the metrics
Only at the very end of the capstone, for the final write-up
questions.explain: Wiring the run into a tracker from the first attempt, with the config attached, makes every run self-describing — exactly the discipline Chapter 4's tracking infrastructure is meant to produce.

questions.q: Why should you decide what "reproduced" means before your run finishes, rather than after you see the number?
options: Because W&B does not allow changing settings mid-run
It has no real effect either way
Because the tracker requires it to be set in advance as a config field
To avoid quietly redefining success after the fact based on how the number happens to land
questions.explain: Pre-committing to a reproduction tier — exact match within noise, tolerance match, or qualitative trend — prevents the standard for success from shifting after you already know the result.

questions.q: If the official, unmodified authors' code fails to reproduce its own claimed number in your environment, what does that most likely indicate?
options: Your GPU is defective
The capstone paper was a bad choice and must be abandoned immediately
An environment or dependency mismatch worth debugging before introducing any of your own code
The official code can simply be ignored from that point on
questions.explain: Running the official code first isolates environment and dependency issues from your own changes — if even the authors' code doesn't match, that's a setup problem to fix first, not evidence to abandon the project.
